newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian churches call for end to race row.
newsitem.headline: Australian churches call for end to race row.

text.p: Australian church leaders called on Monday for an end to the "ill-informed, provocative and deeply offensive" race debate engulfing the country, saying Asian-Australians were being physically and verbally abused.
The Anglican and Uniting churches called on Prime Minister John Howard and other political leaders to end the xenophobic debate, warning it would harm the country.

"While it is right to discuss controversial issues in an open and honest way, there is much in the recent debate which has been ill-informed, provocative and deeply offensive," said Sydney's Anglican archbishop Harry Goodhew.

"I have heard that some of our Asian brothers and sisters have been physically and verbally abused -- some spat at while walking down the street," Goodhew said in opening the 44th Sydney Synod of Anglican bishops.
"Others talk of their deep sense of grief at finding themselves rejected in the country they have chosen as their home," he said.
Goodhew said reverting to an Anglo-Celtic monoculture would harm Australia, which ended a whites-only immigration policy in the early 1970s.

Australia became embroiled in a heated debate over immigration and race last month after an independent politican, Pauline Hanson, said the country was being swamped by Asians and called for a halt to immigration.
Asian migrants make up around 4.5 percent of Australia's 18 million population and constitute a quarter of the 100,000 migrants each year.

The debate has at times plunged into xenophobia, with a town mayor last week calling children of inter-racial marriages "mongrels" and another politican warning welfare assistance to Aborigines was creating an "apartheid" system.
Prime Minister Howard has been criticised for failing to show leadership in not ending the xenophobic debate.
Howard has said he opposes racism but Australians have a right to free speech and should be allowed to debate issues such as immigration.
The Uniting Church, Australia's third-largest Christian grouping, said it was gravely alarmed by reports of rising racial abuse and had written to Howard demanding he move to stop the debate.

"It is time for religious and political leaders to give a clear signal to the Australian public that racism will not be tolerated...under the guise of free speech," the Uniting Church said in statement on Monday.
"For Anglo-Australians to suggest that one racial group has more right to live here than people of other racial backgrounds is outrageous," the church said.
"We are profoundly concerned that the prime minister and leaders within the government have not rejected the factual inaccuracies and insidious implications of Ms Hanson's assertions."
Former prime minister Malcom Fraser on Monday said the current race debate threatened Australia's standing in the Asia-Pacific region.
"I believe it's extraordinarily dangerous for the future of Australia," Fraser told Australian Broadcasting Corp radio.
"I believe the debate is more serious than at any time since I began in politics..." Fraser said.
